title: Optics calculation drill with worked steps
description: Practice 34 standard optics and photonics calculations with new numbers each time: Snell’s law, critical angle, thin lenses, diffraction limit, gratings, Fresnel reflectance, AR coatings, Gaussian beams, fiber NA and V number, dBm, responsivity, photon energy and more. Answers are marked with units, with worked steps and common mistakes.
lead: Standard calculation problems from optics and photonics courses and exams, with new numbers every time. Solve each one yourself and enter the answer with its unit: you will see whether it is right, the worked steps showing which values go into which formula, and the common mistake your number points to. Where a calculator covers the type, you can open it with the same numbers to check.
note: The numbers are practice values drawn from ranges each time. Refractive indices and constants come from the same sources as the formula sheet (listed below) or are stated in the problem as assumptions. For real design work, use values from manufacturers’ data sheets and standards.

groups.quantum: Photons, quantum optics and solar cells

p: Choose a field or a problem type, then start one problem at a time or a set of 5 or 10. With “More of my weak types”, types you last got wrong or often get wrong come up more often. Click a type name in the list of problem types below to get one problem of that type.

Enter the answer as a number and pick the unit from the menu. Forms such as 1.23e-5, 1.23×10^-5 and 1.23 × 10⁻⁵ are all accepted. When you can choose the unit, any unit works (nm or µm, for example) as long as the number matches the unit you chose.

Press “Check” to see the verdict and the worked steps. If you are wrong, the drill shows the common mistake your number points to (radius versus diameter, amplitude versus intensity, θ versus 2θ, 10 versus 20 in decibels and so on). “Show answer” opens the worked steps without answering.

“Copy link to this problem” gives a URL that opens the same problem with the same numbers. The URL holds only the problem type and a seed, never the answer. Your record is saved only in this browser (localStorage) and is never sent to a server. If your browser blocks storage, you can still solve problems; your record just is not kept.

Start by writing down the given values and the quantity you want, with symbols and units. Words in the problem such as “core diameter”, “full angle” or “spectral FWHM” may differ from the quantity in the formula (radius a, half-angle θ, Δλ), so fix them first.
Check where each angle is measured from. In Snell’s law, the critical angle and Brewster’s angle, angles are measured from the surface normal. Watch for degree/radian mix-ups on your calculator.
Keep intensity (power) and amplitude (field) apart. Reflectance R is the square of the amplitude coefficient r, the intensity through a polarizer goes as cos²θ, and dB is 10 log₁₀ of a power ratio.

When you have an answer, check its size. One glass surface reflects about 4 %, visible photons carry 2–3 eV, the V number of a single-mode fiber at 1550 nm is around 2, and the mode spacing of a He–Ne laser is a few hundred MHz. If you are off by a factor of 10 or more, suspect a unit conversion or a power of 10.

The unit menu offers other units for the same quantity (nm and µm, GHz and MHz, mW and µW, ° and rad or mrad, and so on). A correct value in the chosen unit is marked correct. If there is only one unit, answer in that unit.
Fractions can be entered as a decimal from 0 to 1 or in % (0.04 and 4 % are the same). dB and dBm are logarithmic units, so they are not converted to mW or plain ratios.
Temperatures can be entered in K or °C. They are converted by adding or subtracting 273.15.
Common conversions: 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m, 1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m, 1 THz = 10¹² Hz, 1 mrad = 10⁻³ rad ≈ 0.0573°, 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, E[eV] ≈ 1239.84/λ[nm], 1 mW = 0 dBm.

The numbers in each problem are rounded to the digits shown, and the reference answer is computed from those rounded numbers. If you use the numbers as given, rounding will never make your answer wrong.

Marking uses relative error. Most types accept answers within ±1 %. Types answered as an angle (refraction, critical, Brewster, diffraction and acceptance angles) and types answered as a refractive index accept ±0.5 %. Types answered in dBm or dB also use relative error, so −16.0 dBm allows ±0.16 dB. The tolerance is shown with each problem.
Giving the answer to the number of digits used in the problem (usually three significant figures) is enough. More digits are fine too.

If you are just outside the tolerance (within 5 %), the drill says “Close”. The formula is usually right, so check whether you rounded intermediate values too much or used a constant (c, h, q and so on) different from the one in the problem.

faq: My answer should be right, but it is marked wrong.

First check the unit menu. If the unit you chose does not match the number you entered, even a correct value is marked wrong (in most cases you will see “This looks like a unit mix-up”). If the unit matches and you are only slightly off, you probably rounded intermediate values too much or used a different constant. Recalculate with the numbers and constants in the problem, keeping at least four digits along the way.

For each type we set a range that occurs in real components and experiments and draw from it each time. Refractive indices are the same values as in the formula sheet examples (SCHOTT data for N-BK7 and F2, the Malitson Sellmeier equation for fused silica, the Jundt equation for LiNbO₃ and so on). Values that vary, such as birefringence or fiber dispersion, are chosen from a range and stated as assumptions in the problem.
Can I solve the same problem again, or give a friend the same problem?
Yes. Open the URL from “Copy link to this problem” (?t=type&s=seed) and you get the same problem with the same numbers. The URL does not contain the answer, so you can use it to quiz each other.
Where is my record saved? Can I delete it?

Only in this browser’s localStorage; it is never sent to a server and is not shared with other devices or browsers. “Clear record” deletes it. In private browsing or other modes that block storage, no record is kept, but you can still solve problems normally.
What do I get by opening the calculator?

The calculator opens with the same numbers filled in, so you can check the answer another way or see what changes when you vary the conditions. For a Gaussian beam problem you can see the beam radius at other distances z; for an AR coating problem, the reflectance away from the design wavelength. For types without a calculator, the drill links to related terms and the formula sheet.
My textbook answer is slightly different.

Textbooks often round intermediate values or shorten constants (hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm, c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s and so on), so the third digit can differ. The answers here are computed from the numbers and constants in the problem without intermediate rounding. Within the tolerance, either answer is marked correct.

sources.name: Refractive indices (visible, d line 587.6 nm)
sources.text: N-BK7 1.5168 and F2 1.6200 (SCHOTT data sheets), fused silica 1.4585 (Malitson 1965 Sellmeier equation), water 1.333. These match the Sellmeier and Abbe number examples in the formula sheet.

sources.name: Refractive indices (near infrared, 1550 nm)
sources.text: Fused silica 1.4440 and N-BK7 1.5007 (same Sellmeier equations), Si 3.48, LiNbO₃ extraordinary ray 2.138 (Jundt 1997), GaAs 3.37 (Skauli et al. 2003 equation). The group index of fused silica, 1.4626, matches the group index example in the formula sheet.

sources.name: LiNbO₃ indices for SHG
sources.text: Fundamental and second-harmonic values from the Sellmeier equation for the extraordinary ray of congruent LiNbO₃ at 24.5 °C, D. H. Jundt, Opt. Lett. 22, 1553 (1997) (2.1558/2.2342 at 1064/532 nm, for example).

sources.name: Abbe numbers and glasses
sources.text: N-BK7 V_d = 64.17 and F2 V_d = 36.37 (from n_d, n_F and n_C in the SCHOTT data sheets).

sources.name: Birefringence of quartz and MgF₂
sources.text: n_e − n_o at each wavelength from the Sellmeier equations of G. Ghosh, Opt. Commun. 163, 95 (1999) for quartz and M. J. Dodge, Appl. Opt. 23, 1980 (1984) for MgF₂ (for example 0.00904 for quartz and 0.01178 for MgF₂ at 633 nm).

sources.name: Physical constants
sources.text: CODATA 2022 exact and recommended values (c = 299 792 458 m/s, h = 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, q = 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, Wien’s displacement constant b = 2.897 772 × 10⁻³ m·K, hc = 1239.84 eV·nm).

sources.name: Band gaps (room temperature)
sources.text: Si 1.12 eV, Ge 0.66 eV, GaAs 1.42 eV, InP 1.34 eV, In₀.₅₃Ga₀.₄₇As 0.75 eV, GaN 3.4 eV (values from Sze & Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices, 3rd ed., and similar).

sources.name: Fiber and link values
sources.text: Single-mode fiber loss of 0.35 dB/km at 1310 nm and 0.20 dB/km at 1550 nm, 0.5 dB per connector and 0.1 dB per splice, the same as the link budget example in the formula sheet (within the ITU-T G.652 range). The dispersion D is chosen from a range for the 1550 nm band and stated as an assumption.

sources.name: Assumed values
sources.text: The index of silicon nitride films, absorption and extinction coefficients, the group index of semiconductor lasers, the V_oc, J_sc and FF of solar cells and the dark current of photodiodes are practice values chosen from ranges that are realistic for those materials and devices. The time–bandwidth products are 0.441 for Gaussian and 0.315 for sech² pulses.

snell-angle.name: Refraction angle (Snell’s law)
snell-angle.short: Find the refraction angle at a boundary between two media from the angle of incidence
snell-angle.q: Light of wavelength {lam} nm goes from {m1} (n₁ = {n1}) into {m2} (n₂ = {n2}) at an angle of incidence of {t1}° (measured from the surface normal). Find the refraction angle θ₂.
steps: From Snell’s law n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂: sinθ₂ = n₁ sinθ₁/n₂.

mistakes.swap: You swapped n₁ and n₂ (sinθ₂ = n₂ sinθ₁/n₁). n₁ is the index of the medium the light comes from.
mistakes.surf: You gave the angle from the surface (90° − θ₂). Angles are measured from the normal.
mistakes.surfin: You treated the angle of incidence as measured from the surface (cos instead of sin). The given angle is from the normal.

critical-angle.name: Critical angle for total internal reflection
critical-angle.short: Find the critical angle for light hitting a boundary from the denser side, or the index from a measured critical angle

q.ang: Light of wavelength {lam} nm travels inside {m1} (n₁ = {n1}) towards the boundary with {m2} (n₂ = {n2}). Find the critical angle θ_c for total internal reflection.
q.n: Light inside a transparent material hits a flat boundary with {out} (n₂ = {n2}). Total internal reflection starts at an angle of incidence (critical angle) of {tc}°, measured from the normal. Find the refractive index n₁ of the material.

ang: At the critical angle the refraction angle is 90°: n₁ sinθ_c = n₂ sin90°, so sinθ_c = n₂/n₁.

mistakes.brew: You used tanθ = n₂/n₁, which is Brewster’s angle. The critical angle is sinθ_c = n₂/n₁.
mistakes.comp: You gave 90° − θ_c. The critical angle is also measured from the normal.
mistakes.cos: You used cos (the form for an angle measured from the surface). The condition is sinθ_c = n₂/n₁.
mistakes.tan: You used tan. The condition is sinθ_c = n₂/n₁.
mistakes.inv: You computed n₂ × sinθ_c. It is n₁ = n₂/sinθ_c (total internal reflection happens from the higher-index side).

thin-lens.name: Thin lens: image distance and magnification
thin-lens.short: Find the image distance or lateral magnification of a converging lens from its focal length and the object distance

q.b: An object is placed a = {a} mm in front of a converging thin lens (in air) of focal length f = {f} mm. Find the distance b from the lens to the image.
q.m: An object is placed a = {a} mm in front of a converging thin lens (in air) of focal length f = {f} mm. Find the lateral magnification m with its sign (negative for an inverted image).

b: b = {b} mm (positive: a real image behind the lens).

mistakes.plus: You used 1/b = 1/f + 1/a. With the object distance a taken as positive, the equation is 1/a + 1/b = 1/f.
mistakes.inv: You used m = −a/b. The magnification is image size/object size = −b/a.
mistakes.nosign: The size is right but the sign is not. The real image of a converging lens is inverted, so m is negative.

two-lens.name: Two separated lenses: combined focal length
two-lens.short: Find the effective focal length and back focal distance of two thin lenses separated by a gap

q.f: Two thin lenses with focal lengths f₁ = {f1} mm and f₂ = {f2} mm are placed on the same axis d = {d} mm apart (in air). Find the combined focal length f.
q.bfd: Two thin lenses with focal lengths f₁ = {f1} mm and f₂ = {f2} mm are placed on the same axis d = {d} mm apart (in air; light enters through lens 1). Find the distance from lens 2 to the back focal point (back focal distance).

mistakes.nod: You dropped the gap term (that is the formula for lenses in contact, 1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂).
mistakes.plus: You added the d/(f₁f₂) term. Separating two converging lenses lowers the combined power, so it is subtracted.
mistakes.f: You gave the combined focal length f. The back focal distance is measured from lens 2: f(1 − d/f₁).
mistakes.f2: You used f(1 − d/f₂). The back focal distance uses f₁ of the first lens the light meets: f(1 − d/f₁).

na-fnumber.name: Numerical aperture and f-number
na-fnumber.short: Find the NA of an objective, or the f-number and image-side NA from focal length and aperture
na-fnumber.formula: NA = n sinθ, N = f/D, NA ≈ 1/(2N)

q.na: An objective used in {im} (n = {n}) has a marginal-ray half-angle of θ = {th}° on the object side. Find its numerical aperture NA.
q.fn: A lens with focal length f = {f} mm and entrance pupil diameter D = {D} mm images an object at infinity. From the f-number N = f/D, find the image-side numerical aperture using NA ≈ 1/(2N) (assume the lens obeys the sine condition).

mistakes.non: You left out the refractive index n of the medium (NA = n sinθ). With immersion, NA can exceed 1.
mistakes.tan: You used tanθ. The numerical aperture is n sinθ.
mistakes.n1: You gave 1/N. The marginal ray height is D/2, so NA ≈ 1/(2N).
mistakes.atan: You took sinθ of θ = arctan(D/(2f)). For a lens that obeys the sine condition the marginal ray height is f sinθ, so sinθ = D/(2f).
mistakes.nval: You gave the f-number N. The question asks for NA ≈ 1/(2N).

young-fringe.name: Fringe spacing in Young’s experiment
young-fringe.short: Find the fringe spacing of a double slit, or the wavelength from a measured spacing

q.dy: In Young’s double-slit experiment the slits are d = {d} mm apart and the screen is L = {L} m away. Light of wavelength {lam} nm is used. Find the spacing Δy between neighboring bright fringes on the screen.
q.lam: Two slits d = {d} mm apart illuminate a screen L = {L} m away. The distance from one bright fringe to the bright fringe {N} fringes further on is {s} mm. Find the wavelength of the light.

dy: For L ≫ d the spacing of neighboring bright fringes is Δy = λL/d.
lam: Spacing of neighboring bright fringes Δy = {s}/{N} = {dy} mm.

mistakes.half: You have a stray factor of 2 (Δy = λL/(2d) or 2λL/d). The fringe spacing is Δy = λL/d, with no 2.
mistakes.dbl: You multiplied by 2. The path difference changes by λ from one bright fringe to the next, so Δy = λL/d.
mistakes.non: You did not divide by {N}. {s} mm spans {N} fringe spacings.
mistakes.n1: You divided by {N} − 1. From one bright fringe to the one {N} fringes further on there are {N} spacings.

airy-spot.name: Diffraction limit (Airy disk and Rayleigh criterion)
airy-spot.short: Find the angular resolution of a telescope, the Airy disk radius of a focused spot, or the resolution of a microscope

q.ang: A telescope with aperture D = {D} mm observes light of wavelength {lam} nm. Find the smallest angle θ_R between two point sources that can be resolved by the Rayleigh criterion.
q.spot: An aberration-free lens of f-number N = {N} focuses a collimated beam of wavelength {lam} nm. Find the radius of the Airy disk in the focal plane (from the center to the first dark ring).
q.res: A microscope objective with NA = {na} is used with light of wavelength {lam} nm. Find the resolution by the Rayleigh criterion (smallest separation of two points that can be resolved).

ang: For diffraction by a circular aperture the first dark ring is at sinθ_R = 1.22λ/D (θ_R ≈ 1.22λ/D for small angles).
spot: The Airy disk radius in the focal plane is r = 1.22λf/D = 1.22λN.
res: Rayleigh criterion: the center of one image falls on the first dark ring of the other, at δ = 0.61λ/NA.

mistakes.no122: You dropped the factor 1.22. For a circular aperture the first dark ring is at 1.22λ/D (1.22 is the first zero of the Bessel function J₁, 3.832, divided by π).
mistakes.diam: You gave the diameter of the first dark ring. The question asks for the distance from the center to the first dark ring.
mistakes.abbe: You gave the Abbe limit λ/(2NA). The Rayleigh criterion is 0.61λ/NA.

grating-angle.name: Diffraction grating: angle and resolving power
grating-angle.short: Find the diffraction angle for normal incidence on a grating, or the smallest wavelength difference it resolves

q.beta: Light of wavelength {lam} nm falls at normal incidence on a grating with {G} lines per mm. Find the diffraction angle β of the order m = {m} (measured from the grating normal).
q.dl: A grating with {G} lines per mm is illuminated over its full width of {W} mm by light near {lam} nm. Find the smallest wavelength difference δλ resolved in order m = {m}.

beta: At normal incidence d sinβ = mλ, so sinβ = mλ/d = {m} × {lam}/{d} = {s}.

mistakes.m1: This is the first-order value. The question asks for order {m} (sinβ = mλ/d, λ/δλ = mN).
mistakes.tan: You used tanβ = mλ/d. The grating equation is d sinβ = mλ.
mistakes.nw: You used the lines per mm, {G}, as N. Multiply by the illuminated width: N = {G} × {W}.

fsr-finesse.name: Fabry–Perot: FSR, finesse and linewidth
fsr-finesse.short: Find the free spectral range of an etalon, the finesse from the mirror reflectance, or the linewidth of a transmission peak
fsr-finesse.formula: Δν_FSR = c/(2n_g L), 𝓕 = π√R/(1 − R), δν = Δν_FSR/𝓕

q.fsr: A Fabry–Perot etalon of {med} (group index n_g = {ng}) has a mirror spacing of L = {L} mm. Find the free spectral range Δν_FSR in frequency (c = {c} m/s, normal incidence).
q.fin: Both mirrors of a Fabry–Perot cavity have reflectance R = {R} (no absorption or scattering loss). Find the finesse 𝓕.
q.lw: A Fabry–Perot etalon of {med} (group index n_g = {ng}) has a mirror spacing of L = {L} mm and mirror reflectance R = {R}. Find the full width at half maximum δν of a transmission peak (c = {c} m/s, normal incidence, no loss).

mistakes.no2: The factor 2 is missing (or doubled). Light makes a round trip between the mirrors, so Δν_FSR = c/(2n_g L).
mistakes.non: You left out the group index n_g (unless the gap is air, the optical path is n_g times longer).
mistakes.coef: You gave the coefficient F = 4R/(1 − R)². The finesse 𝓕 = π√R/(1 − R) is a different quantity (𝓕 = (π/2)√F).
mistakes.nosq: You used R instead of √R (𝓕 = π√R/(1 − R)).
mistakes.nopi: You left out π (𝓕 = π√R/(1 − R)).
mistakes.mult: You multiplied Δν_FSR by 𝓕. The linewidth is Δν_FSR divided by 𝓕 (higher finesse gives sharper peaks).
mistakes.fsr: You gave the free spectral range. The linewidth is δν = Δν_FSR/𝓕.

coherence-length.name: Coherence length
coherence-length.short: Estimate the coherence length from the spectral width of a source (in wavelength or frequency)

q.lam: A broadband source (such as an SLD) has a center wavelength of {lam} nm and a spectral FWHM of Δλ = {dl} nm. Find its coherence length using l_c ≈ λ²/Δλ.
q.nu: A laser has a spectral linewidth of Δν = {dnu} MHz. Find its coherence length using l_c ≈ c/Δν (c = {c} m/s).

mistakes.half: You divided by 2. In an interferometer with a round trip the mirror moves by l_c/2, but the coherence length itself is λ²/Δλ (c/Δν).
mistakes.oct: You gave (2 ln2/π)λ²/Δλ, the OCT axial resolution for a Gaussian spectrum. This question uses l_c ≈ λ²/Δλ.
mistakes.pi: You gave c/(πΔν), another definition used for a Lorentzian line. This question uses l_c ≈ c/Δν.

brewster.name: Brewster’s angle
brewster.short: Find the angle of incidence at which p-polarized light is not reflected, from the two refractive indices
brewster.q: Light of wavelength {lam} nm goes from {m1} (n₁ = {n1}) onto a flat boundary with {m2} (n₂ = {n2}). Find the angle of incidence θ_B at which the reflectance for p-polarization is zero (Brewster’s angle).
steps: The refraction angle is then 90° − θ_B = {tt}°, so the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular.

mistakes.inv: You used n₁/n₂. It is tanθ_B = n₂/n₁, where n₁ is the index of the medium the light comes from.
mistakes.crit: You used sinθ = (lower index)/(higher index), which is the critical angle. Brewster’s angle is tanθ_B = n₂/n₁.

fresnel-normal.name: Reflectance at normal incidence (Fresnel)
fresnel-normal.short: Find the reflectance of one surface at normal incidence, the transmission through a plate, or the index from a measured reflectance

q.r: Light of wavelength {lam} nm goes from {m1} (n₁ = {n1}) onto a flat surface of {m2} (n₂ = {n2}) at normal incidence. Find the intensity reflectance R.
q.t2: Light of wavelength {lam} nm hits a plane-parallel plate of {m2} (n = {n2}) in air at normal incidence. Considering only the reflections at the two surfaces (ignore multiple reflections inside the plate and absorption), find the fraction of light that passes through the plate.
q.n: Light hits a flat surface of a non-absorbing material in air at normal incidence, and the intensity reflectance is {R} %. Find the refractive index n of the material.

r: Amplitude reflection coefficient at normal incidence r = (n₁ − n₂)/(n₁ + n₂) = {r}.

mistakes.amp: You gave the amplitude coefficient |r|. The intensity reflectance is its square, R = r².
mistakes.trans: You gave the transmittance 1 − R. The question asks for the reflectance.
mistakes.one: That is 1 − R for one surface. The plate has two surfaces.
mistakes.mult: That is (1 − R)/(1 + R), which includes multiple reflections inside the plate. This question ignores them: (1 − R)².
mistakes.r: You gave the reflectance R of one surface. The question asks for the fraction that passes through the plate.
mistakes.nosqrt: You used (1 + R)/(1 − R) without the square root. √R = (n − 1)/(n + 1).
mistakes.inv: You used (1 − √R)/(1 + √R). The index is the value above 1, (1 + √R)/(1 − √R).

malus.name: Malus’s law (light through polarizers)
malus.short: Find the power after linearly polarized or unpolarized light passes through one or more polarizers

q.pol: Linearly polarized light with a power of {I0} mW passes through an ideal polarizer whose transmission axis is at θ = {th}° to the polarization. Find the transmitted power.
q.unpol: Unpolarized light with a power of {I0} mW passes through two ideal polarizers whose transmission axes are {th}° apart. Find the power after the second polarizer.
q.three: Unpolarized light with a power of {I0} mW passes in turn through three ideal polarizers with transmission axes at 0°, {th}° and 90°. Find the power after the third polarizer.

unpol: The first polarizer passes half of unpolarized light: {I0}/2 = {h} mW.
Malus’s law at the second: cos²{th}° = {c2}.
three: Half passes the first polarizer: {h} mW.
Second ({th}° from the first): multiply by cos²{th}° = {c2} to get {I2} mW.
Third ({th3}° from the second): multiply by cos²{th3}° = sin²{th}° = {s2} to get {I} mW.

mistakes.nosq: You did not square cosθ. The field amplitude scales by cosθ and the intensity by cos²θ.
mistakes.sin: You used sin²θ. θ is the angle between the polarization and the transmission axis, and the transmitted fraction is cos²θ.
mistakes.nohalf: You forgot that the first polarizer passes only half of unpolarized light.
mistakes.one: That is the power after the second polarizer. The third is {th3}° from the second, so multiply by cos²{th3}° as well.
mistakes.zero: Zero is the result with only the 0° and 90° polarizers. With the {th}° polarizer in between, light gets through.

waveplate.name: Wave plate thickness and retardance
waveplate.short: Find the thickness of a zero-order quarter- or half-wave plate, or the retardance of a birefringent plate in waves

q.qwp: A zero-order quarter-wave plate for {lam} nm is made of {x} (take n_e − n_o = {dn} at {lam} nm). Find the plate thickness d.
q.hwp: A zero-order half-wave plate for {lam} nm is made of {x} (take n_e − n_o = {dn} at {lam} nm). Find the plate thickness d.
q.ret: A plate of {x} (take n_e − n_o = {dn} at {lam} nm), {d} mm thick with the optic axis in the plane of the plate, is used at normal incidence. Find its retardance at {lam} nm in waves (Γ/2π).

qwp: For a quarter-wave plate the optical path difference (n_e − n_o)d of the two polarizations is λ/4.
hwp: For a half-wave plate the optical path difference (n_e − n_o)d is λ/2.
ret: Optical path difference (n_e − n_o)d = {dn} × {d} mm = {od} nm.

mistakes.half: λ/(2Δn) is the thickness of a half-wave plate. A quarter-wave plate is λ/(4Δn).
mistakes.quarter: λ/(4Δn) is the thickness of a quarter-wave plate. A half-wave plate is λ/(2Δn).
mistakes.full: That is λ/Δn, the thickness for a full wave (retardance 2π).
mistakes.nodn: You did not divide by the birefringence n_e − n_o. λ/4 and λ/2 are path differences; the thickness is that divided by n_e − n_o.
mistakes.rad: You gave the retardance in radians (Γ = 2π × {w}). The question asks for it in waves (Γ/2π).

ar-coat.name: Quarter-wave AR coating: thickness, index and reflectance
ar-coat.short: Find the physical thickness of a single-layer quarter-wave antireflection coating, the ideal coating index, or the reflectance at the design wavelength
ar-coat.formula: d = λ₀/(4n₁), n₁ = √(n₀nₛ), R = ((n₀nₛ − n₁²)/(n₀nₛ + n₁²))²

q.d: A single-layer antireflection coating of {film} (n₁ = {n1}) is applied to a substrate of {s} (nₛ = {ns}) as a quarter-wave layer for the design wavelength λ₀ = {lam0} nm. Find the physical thickness d of the coating (in air, normal incidence).
q.n: A single-layer quarter-wave antireflection coating for use in air (n₀ = 1) is applied to a substrate of {s} (nₛ = {ns} at {lam0} nm). Find the ideal coating index n₁ that gives zero reflectance at the design wavelength.
q.r: A quarter-wave layer of {film} (n₁ = {n1}, design wavelength {lam0} nm) is applied to a substrate of {s} (nₛ = {ns}). Find the reflectance of the surface at the design wavelength and normal incidence (in air, n₀ = 1).

d: Make the optical thickness n₁d equal to λ₀/4: n₁d = {lam0}/4 = {opt} nm.
n: The two reflections have equal amplitude when n₁ = √(n₀nₛ).
r: Reflectance of a quarter-wave layer at the design wavelength: R = ((n₀nₛ − n₁²)/(n₀nₛ + n₁²))².

mistakes.nodiv: λ₀/4 is the optical thickness. Inside the layer the wavelength shrinks to λ₀/n₁, so the physical thickness is λ₀/(4n₁).
mistakes.half: λ₀/(2n₁) is a half-wave layer. At the design wavelength a half-wave layer reflects as if there were no coating.
mistakes.ns: You divided by the substrate index. The thickness depends on the coating index n₁ (d = λ₀/(4n₁)).
mistakes.mean: You took the arithmetic mean of n₀ and nₛ. The ideal index is the geometric mean √(n₀nₛ).
mistakes.nosqrt: You did not take the square root (n₁ = √(n₀nₛ)).
mistakes.bare: That is the reflectance without the coating, ((nₛ − 1)/(nₛ + 1))².
mistakes.amp: You gave the amplitude coefficient. The intensity reflectance is its square.
mistakes.simple: That is ((nₛ − n₁)/(nₛ + n₁))² for the coating–substrate boundary alone. A quarter-wave layer combines both reflections: ((n₀nₛ − n₁²)/(n₀nₛ + n₁²))².

achromat.name: Achromatic doublet: focal lengths of the two lenses
achromat.short: Find the focal length of each lens of a cemented crown–flint achromatic doublet
achromat.formula: φ₁/V₁ + φ₂/V₂ = 0, φ₁ = φV₁/(V₁ − V₂), φ₂ = −φV₂/(V₁ − V₂)

q.f1: A converging lens of N-BK7 (Abbe number V₁ = {V1}) and a diverging lens of F2 (V₂ = {V2}) are cemented into an achromatic doublet (C and F lines brought to the same focus) with a combined focal length f = {f} mm. Find the focal length f₁ of the N-BK7 lens.
q.f2: A converging lens of N-BK7 (Abbe number V₁ = {V1}) and a diverging lens of F2 (V₂ = {V2}) are cemented into an achromatic doublet (C and F lines brought to the same focus) with a combined focal length f = {f} mm. Find the focal length f₂ of the F2 lens, with its sign.

f1: From the achromat condition φ₁/V₁ + φ₂/V₂ = 0 and φ₁ + φ₂ = φ: φ₁ = φV₁/(V₁ − V₂).
f2: From the achromat condition φ₁/V₁ + φ₂/V₂ = 0 and φ₁ + φ₂ = φ: φ₂ = −φV₂/(V₁ − V₂).

mistakes.inv: You mixed up the power φ and the focal length f = 1/φ (from φ₁ = φV₁/(V₁ − V₂), f₁ = f(V₁ − V₂)/V₁).

absorption.name: Absorption coefficient and transmittance (Beer–Lambert)
absorption.short: Find the internal transmittance from α and thickness, the 1/e penetration depth, or α from the extinction coefficient

q.trans: A plate of a material with absorption coefficient α = {a} cm⁻¹ is {z} mm thick. Find its internal transmittance I/I₀ (excluding surface reflections).
q.depth: In a material with absorption coefficient α = {a} cm⁻¹, find the depth at which the intensity falls to 1/e (about 37 %) of its incident value.
q.kappa: A material has an extinction coefficient (imaginary part of the complex index) κ = {kap}. Find the intensity absorption coefficient α at {lam} nm.

mistakes.log10: You used 10^(−αz). In the Beer–Lambert law α goes with the natural exponential e^(−αz) (base 10 is for absorbance).
mistakes.cm: You multiplied α in cm⁻¹ by the thickness in mm. Convert z to cm first (1 mm = 0.1 cm).
mistakes.lin: You used the approximation 1 − αz. αz is not small here, so use e^(−αz).
mistakes.ln2: That is ln2/α, where the intensity halves. It falls to 1/e at 1/α.
mistakes.amp: That is 2/α, where the field amplitude falls to 1/e. Intensity is the square of the amplitude, so the answer is 1/α.
mistakes.pi2: 2πκ/λ is the amplitude attenuation coefficient. The intensity coefficient is twice that, 4πκ/λ.

gauss-beam.name: Gaussian beam: zR, w(z) and divergence
gauss-beam.short: From the beam waist and M², find the Rayleigh range, the beam radius at a distance z, or the far-field divergence
gauss-beam.formula: z_R = πw₀²/(M²λ), w(z) = w₀√(1 + (z/z_R)²), θ = M²λ/(πw₀)

q.zr: A laser beam (in air) has a wavelength of {lam} nm, a waist radius w₀ = {w0} µm (1/e²) and M² = {m2}. Find the Rayleigh range z_R.
q.wz: A laser beam (in air) has a wavelength of {lam} nm, a waist radius w₀ = {w0} µm (1/e²) and M² = {m2}. Find the beam radius w(z) at z = {z} mm from the waist.
q.div: A laser beam (in air) has a wavelength of {lam} nm, a waist radius w₀ = {w0} µm (1/e²) and M² = {m2}. Find the far-field divergence half-angle θ.

mistakes.diam: You used the diameter for w₀. w₀ is the radius (to the 1/e² intensity point).
mistakes.nopi: You left out π (z_R = πw₀²/(M²λ), θ = M²λ/(πw₀)).
mistakes.m2: M² is applied the wrong way. A higher M² shortens z_R (by 1/M²) and increases θ (by M²).
mistakes.full: You gave the full angle 2θ. The question asks for the half-angle.
mistakes.nosqrt: You forgot the square root (w = w₀√(1 + (z/z_R)²)).
mistakes.far: You used the far-field approximation w ≈ w₀z/z_R (= θz). Within a few z_R of the waist use √(1 + (z/z_R)²).
mistakes.lin: You used w₀(1 + z/z_R). It is w₀√(1 + (z/z_R)²).

long-modes.name: Longitudinal mode spacing
long-modes.short: Find the frequency spacing of longitudinal modes from the cavity length, or the wavelength spacing of a semiconductor laser

q.nu: A He–Ne laser has a cavity length L = {L} m (take the index inside the cavity as 1). Find the frequency spacing Δν of its longitudinal modes (c = {c} m/s).
q.lam: A Fabry–Perot semiconductor laser has a length L = {Lu} µm and group index n_g = {ng}. Find the wavelength spacing Δλ of its longitudinal modes near {lam} nm.

mistakes.no2: You dropped the 2. Light makes a round trip in the cavity, so Δν = c/(2nL) and Δλ = λ²/(2n_g L).
mistakes.half: You divided by 4L. It is Δν = c/(2nL).
mistakes.non: You left out the group index n_g.

fiber-na.name: Fiber NA, acceptance angle and index contrast
fiber-na.short: From the core and cladding indices, find the numerical aperture, the acceptance angle in air or the relative index difference

q.na: A step-index fiber has a core index n₁ = {n1} and a cladding index n₂ = {n2}. Find its numerical aperture NA.
q.theta: Light is launched from air into the end face of a step-index fiber with core index n₁ = {n1} and cladding index n₂ = {n2}. Find the largest angle of incidence θ_max (acceptance half-angle) for light guided in the core.
q.delta: A step-index fiber has a core index n₁ = {n1} and a cladding index n₂ = {n2}. Find the relative index difference Δ = (n₁² − n₂²)/(2n₁²).

theta: In air (n₀ = 1) sinθ_max = NA, so θ_max = arcsin {na} = {th}°.

mistakes.diff: You gave n₁ − n₂. NA = √(n₁² − n₂²).
mistakes.nosqrt: You did not take the square root (NA = √(n₁² − n₂²)).
mistakes.nosq: You used √(n₁ − n₂). It is the square root of the difference of squares, n₁² − n₂².
mistakes.full: You gave the full angle 2θ_max. The question asks for the half-angle.
mistakes.core: That is the angle inside the core, arcsin(NA/n₁). In air sinθ_max = NA.
mistakes.no2: You did not divide by 2 (Δ = (n₁² − n₂²)/(2n₁²)).
mistakes.na: You gave the numerical aperture NA.

v-number.name: Fiber V number and cutoff wavelength
v-number.short: Find the normalized frequency V from core size, indices and wavelength, or the cutoff wavelength for single-mode operation

q.v: A step-index fiber with core index n₁ = {n1}, cladding index n₂ = {n2} and core diameter {dc} µm is used at {lam} nm. Find the normalized frequency V.
q.lc: A step-index fiber has core index n₁ = {n1}, cladding index n₂ = {n2} and core diameter {dc} µm. Find its cutoff wavelength λ_c (single-mode at longer wavelengths).

lc: NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) = {na}; core radius a = {dc}/2 = {a} µm.

mistakes.diam: You used the core diameter as a. a is the core radius (half the diameter).

chrom-disp.name: Pulse broadening by chromatic dispersion
chrom-disp.short: Find the pulse broadening from dispersion, length and spectral width, or the maximum length for an allowed broadening

q.tau: A light pulse with spectral width Δλ = {dl} nm travels L = {L} km in a fiber with dispersion D = {D} ps/(nm·km) (1550 nm band). Find the broadening Δτ.
q.nu: Light at 1550 nm with a spectral width Δν = {dnu} GHz is sent over L = {L} km of fiber with dispersion D = {D} ps/(nm·km). Find the pulse broadening Δτ due to chromatic dispersion (c = {c} m/s).
q.len: Pulses with spectral width Δλ = {dl} nm are sent through a fiber with dispersion D = {D} ps/(nm·km). Find the maximum length for which the dispersive broadening stays at or below {tau} ps.

nu: Convert the frequency width to wavelength: Δλ = λ²Δν/c = (1550 nm)² × {dnu} GHz/c = {dlc} nm.
len: From Δτ = |D| L Δλ: L = Δτ/(|D|Δλ).

mistakes.div: You divided by Δλ. The broadening is proportional to Δλ (Δτ = |D| L Δλ).
mistakes.raw: You used the number for Δν in GHz as Δλ in nm. Convert with Δλ = λ²Δν/c (at 1550 nm, 1 GHz ≈ 0.008 nm).
mistakes.mult: You multiplied Δτ × |D| × Δλ. It is L = Δτ/(|D|Δλ).

db-power.name: dBm–mW conversion and fiber loss
db-power.short: Convert optical power between mW and dBm, or find the power after a loss given in dB/km

q.todbm: Express an optical power of {P} mW in dBm.
q.tomw: Express an optical power of {dbm} dBm in mW.
q.loss: {Pin} mW of light is launched into a fiber with a loss of {al} dB/km. Find the optical power after {L} km.

mistakes.ln: You used base e instead of 10. Decibels use the common logarithm (base 10).
mistakes.x20: You used 20 log₁₀ (or 10^(x/20)). Power quantities such as optical power use 10 log₁₀ (20 is for amplitude ratios such as voltage or field).
mistakes.w: You used 1 W as the reference (dBW). dBm is referenced to 1 mW.
mistakes.np: You used the loss in dB directly as an exponent of e. Use P = P₀·10^(−A/10).

link-budget.name: Optical link power budget
link-budget.short: Subtract fiber, connector and splice losses from the launch power to find the received power and the margin
link-budget.formula: P_rx = P_tx − αL − N_cL_c − N_sL_s, M = P_rx − S

q.prx: A transmitter launches {Ptx} dBm into {L} km of single-mode fiber with a loss of {al} dB/km at {w} nm. The link has {Nc} connectors ({Lc} dB each) and {Ns} fusion splices ({Ls} dB each). Find the received power.
q.margin: A transmitter launches {Ptx} dBm into {L} km of single-mode fiber with a loss of {al} dB/km at {w} nm. The link has {Nc} connectors ({Lc} dB each) and {Ns} fusion splices ({Ls} dB each). The receiver sensitivity is {S} dBm. Find the power margin.

mistakes.noconn: You left out the connector and splice losses.
mistakes.nosp: You left out the splice loss of {As} dB.
mistakes.plus: You added the losses. Losses in dB are subtracted from the launch power in dBm.
mistakes.prx: You gave the received power P_rx. The margin is the difference from the sensitivity, P_rx − S.

responsivity.name: Photodiode responsivity and quantum efficiency
responsivity.short: Find the responsivity or photocurrent from the quantum efficiency and wavelength, or the quantum efficiency from a measured photocurrent

q.r: A photodiode made of {det} has a quantum efficiency η = {eta} at {lam} nm. Find its responsivity ℛ (q = {e} C, h = {h} J·s, c = {c} m/s).
q.ip: {P} µW of light at {lam} nm falls on a photodiode made of {det} with quantum efficiency η = {eta} at that wavelength. Find the photocurrent (q = {e} C, h = {h} J·s, c = {c} m/s).
q.eta: When {P} µW of light at {lam} nm falls on a photodiode made of {det}, the photocurrent is {I} µA. Find the quantum efficiency η (q = {e} C, h = {h} J·s, c = {c} m/s).

r: Responsivity at unit quantum efficiency qλ/(hc) = {r1} A/W (the same as λ[nm]/1239.84).
ip: Responsivity at unit quantum efficiency qλ/(hc) = {r1} A/W.

mistakes.noeta: You left out the quantum efficiency η (this is the upper limit for η = 1).
mistakes.inv: You inverted it (ℛ = ηqλ/(hc), I_p = ℛP).
mistakes.r: You gave the responsivity I_p/P in A/W. The quantum efficiency is that divided by qλ/(hc).

shot-noise.name: Shot noise current
shot-noise.short: Find the rms shot noise current from the photocurrent, dark current and bandwidth
shot-noise.q: A photodiode with a photocurrent of {Ip} µA and a dark current of {Id} nA is used with a bandwidth of {bw} MHz. Find the rms shot noise current (q = {e} C).

mistakes.nodark: You left out the dark current I_d. The dark current also produces shot noise.

shg-coherence.name: SHG coherence length and QPM period
shg-coherence.short: From the fundamental and second-harmonic indices, find the coherence length without phase matching and the poling period of PPLN

q.lc: The second harmonic ({lam2} nm) of {lam} nm light is generated in LiNbO₃ with extraordinary polarization (24.5 °C). The indices are n(ω) = {n1} and n(2ω) = {n2}. Find the coherence length L_c without phase matching.
q.qpm: The second harmonic ({lam2} nm) of {lam} nm light is generated in LiNbO₃ with extraordinary polarization (24.5 °C). The indices are n(ω) = {n1} and n(2ω) = {n2}. Find the poling period Λ for first-order quasi-phase matching in periodically poled LiNbO₃ (PPLN).

lc: Δk = k₂ω − 2kω = (4π/λ)(n₂ω − nω) (λ is the fundamental wavelength).
L_c = π/Δk = λ/(4(n₂ω − nω)) = {lam} nm/(4 × {dn}) = {lc} µm.

mistakes.qpm: λ/(2Δn) is the QPM period Λ = 2L_c. The coherence length is L_c = λ/(4Δn).
mistakes.lc: You gave the coherence length L_c. The poling period is Λ = 2L_c.
mistakes.nofour: The factor in the denominator is missing (L_c = λ/(4Δn), Λ = λ/(2Δn)).
mistakes.sh: You used the second-harmonic wavelength λ/2. The λ in the formula is the fundamental wavelength.

tbp.name: Time–bandwidth product (transform-limited pulses)
tbp.short: Find the spectral width (in frequency or wavelength) from the pulse duration, or the shortest pulse from the spectral width

q.nu: A transform-limited {sh} pulse (time–bandwidth product K = {K}) has a duration (intensity FWHM) of Δt = {dt} fs. Find its spectral width Δν.
q.lam: A transform-limited {sh} pulse (K = {K}) centered at {lam} nm has a duration of Δt = {dt} fs. Find its spectral width in wavelength, Δλ (c = {c} m/s).
q.dt: Light centered at {lam} nm has a spectral width of Δλ = {dl} nm. Find the duration Δt of the shortest {sh} pulse it can support (transform-limited, K = {K}; c = {c} m/s).

nu: For a transform-limited pulse ΔνΔt = K.

mistakes.shape: You used the K for the other pulse shape (Gaussian 0.441, sech² 0.315).
mistakes.one: You used ΔνΔt = 1. For a transform-limited pulse ΔνΔt = K ({K} for this shape).

spdc-idler.name: Wavelengths in parametric processes (energy conservation)
spdc-idler.short: Find the idler wavelength from the pump and signal wavelengths, or the pump wavelength from the signal and idler

q.idler: A pump at {lp} nm drives parametric down-conversion (or an optical parametric oscillator), and the signal is at {ls} nm. Find the idler wavelength.
q.pump: A parametric process produces a signal at {ls} nm and an idler at {li} nm. Find the pump wavelength.

idler: Energy conservation ω_p = ω_s + ω_i gives 1/λ_p = 1/λ_s + 1/λ_i.
pump: Energy conservation ω_p = ω_s + ω_i gives 1/λ_p = 1/λ_s + 1/λ_i.

mistakes.diff: You gave the wavelength difference λ_s − λ_p. It is the frequencies (1/λ) that add and subtract.
mistakes.deg: That is the degenerate case (signal and idler both at 2λ_p). The signal is at {ls} nm, so the idler is at a different wavelength.
mistakes.minus: You used 1/λ_s − 1/λ_i. For the pump they add: 1/λ_p = 1/λ_s + 1/λ_i.
mistakes.avg: You took half the mean of the signal and idler wavelengths, (λ_s + λ_i)/4. That only works near degeneracy. The exact relation is 1/λ_p = 1/λ_s + 1/λ_i: the 1/λ (frequencies) add.

wien.name: Wien’s displacement law
wien.short: Find the peak wavelength of blackbody radiation from the temperature, or the temperature from the peak

q.lam: Find the wavelength λ_max at which a blackbody at {T} K radiates most strongly (peak of the spectrum per unit wavelength; b = {b} m·K).
q.tc: An object heated to {tc} °C is treated as a blackbody. Find the wavelength λ_max at which it radiates most strongly (peak of the spectrum per unit wavelength; b = {b} m·K).
q.temp: The spectrum per unit wavelength of a source that behaves as a blackbody peaks at {lm} µm. Find its temperature (b = {b} m·K).

lam: Wien’s displacement law: λ_max T = b.
tc: Convert to absolute temperature: T = {tc} + 273.15 = {TK} K.

mistakes.nupeak: That comes from the peak of the spectrum per unit frequency (ν_max = 5.879 × 10¹⁰ Hz/K × T). The per-wavelength peak is λ_max T = b (the two peaks are not at the same wavelength).
mistakes.celsius: You used the Celsius number directly. Use the absolute temperature T = t + 273.15.

illuminance.name: Illuminance (inverse square and cosine law)
illuminance.short: Find the illuminance from the luminous intensity of a point source, the distance and the tilt of the surface

q.n: Find the illuminance on a surface facing a point source of {I} cd from {d} m away.
q.tilt: A surface is {d} m from a point source of {I} cd, and its normal is tilted {th}° from the direction of the source. Find the illuminance on the surface.

n: Illuminance E = I cosθ/d² (facing the source, cosθ = 1).

mistakes.nosq: You did not square the distance (inverse square law, E ∝ 1/d²).
mistakes.nocos: You left out cosθ for the tilt of the surface.
mistakes.sin: You used sinθ. θ is the angle between the surface normal and the light, so multiply by cosθ.

photon-energy.name: Photon energy, frequency and wavenumber
photon-energy.short: Find the photon energy (eV), frequency or wavenumber from the wavelength, or the cutoff wavelength from a band gap

q.ev: Find the energy in eV of a photon of wavelength {lam} nm in vacuum (hc = {hc} eV·nm).
q.thz: Find the frequency ν of light of wavelength {lam} nm in vacuum (c = {c} m/s).
q.kayser: Find the wavenumber (waves per cm) of light of wavelength {lam} nm in vacuum, in cm⁻¹.
q.gap: Find the longest wavelength (cutoff wavelength) that a detector made of {m} (band gap {Eg} eV at room temperature) can absorb (hc = {hc} eV·nm).

gap: A photon is absorbed if its energy is at least the band gap: hc/λ ≥ E_g.

mistakes.inv: The formula is upside down. E = hc/λ (shorter wavelength, higher energy) and λ = hc/E.
mistakes.mult: You multiplied E_g by hc. It is λ_c = hc/E_g: the smaller the band gap, the longer the cutoff wavelength.
mistakes.pi2: You multiplied by 2π (angular frequency ω = 2πν or angular wavenumber k = 2π/λ). The frequency ν and the wavenumber σ̃ = 1/λ have no 2π.

photon-flux.name: Photon flux
photon-flux.short: Find the number of photons per second from the power and wavelength, or the power from the photon rate

q.n: Find the number of photons per second Φ carried by light of wavelength {lam} nm and power {P} {pu} (h = {h} J·s, c = {c} m/s).
q.p: Photons of wavelength {lam} nm arrive at a rate of {phi} per second. Find the optical power (h = {h} J·s, c = {c} m/s).

n: Energy of one photon E = hc/λ = {E} J.
p: Energy of one photon E = hc/λ = {E} J.

mistakes.ev: You used the photon energy in eV. To match W (J/s), work in joules (1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J).

solar-ff.name: Solar cell fill factor and efficiency
solar-ff.short: Find the conversion efficiency from V_oc, J_sc and the fill factor, or the fill factor from the maximum power point
solar-ff.formula: FF = V_mp J_mp/(V_oc J_sc), η = FF V_oc J_sc/P_in

q.eta: A {cell} has an open-circuit voltage V_oc = {Voc} V, a short-circuit current density J_sc = {Jsc} mA/cm² and a fill factor FF = {FF}. Find its conversion efficiency η under AM1.5G light (1000 W/m²).
q.ff: A {cell} has V_oc = {Voc} V and J_sc = {Jsc} mA/cm², and its maximum power point is at V_mp = {Vmp} V, J_mp = {Jmp} mA/cm². Find the fill factor FF.

eta: Maximum output P = FF V_oc J_sc = {FF} × {Voc} × {J} = {P} W/m².
ff: V_mp J_mp = {pm} mW/cm², V_oc J_sc = {p0} mW/cm².

mistakes.noff: You left out the fill factor FF (V_oc and J_sc cannot be delivered at the same time).
mistakes.inv: The ratio is upside down. FF is less than 1.
mistakes.v: That is only the voltage ratio V_mp/V_oc. Multiply by the current ratio J_mp/J_sc as well.
mistakes.j: That is only the current ratio J_mp/J_sc. Multiply by the voltage ratio V_mp/V_oc as well.
